title: Avoid blundering: why not blundering is 80% of a winning startup strategy
summary: Jason uses his own chess game data and Simon Ramo's amateur tennis finding to argue that amateur outcomes are mostly decided by errors, not brilliance. He applies this to startups, listing preventable blunders (skipping customer contact, no target audience, premature scaling, coding instead of selling) and separating them from bad luck and non-causes.

principles.text: Amateurs mostly lose by erring, not win by brilliance, so avoiding avoidable mistakes is a large share of winning.
principles.quote: There is a way to build startups with lower risk, in large part by avoiding those blunders

principles.text: Look for the underlying cause of failure, not the proximate one like 'ran out of cash' or 'founder stopped'.
principles.quote: We need to identify the cancer, not just say "the founder stopped."

principles.text: Pick a specific target audience and speak to them; trying to address everyone is a blunder.
principles.quote: Speaking to everyone means speaking to no one.

principles.text: Before product/market fit, discover what works; scaling comes only after, and scaling early wastes time and money.
principles.quote: scaling is about doubling-down on what works--doing it more, faster, better, higher quality, more efficiently.

principles.text: Builders retreat into code because marketing and sales are hard; getting customers requires putting down the compiler.
principles.quote: Coders like to code; everything else is hard, and not fun, and unclear how to execute, and costs money

principles.text: Win your target market before expanding to a second segment or product; premature expansion dilutes focus.
principles.quote: This blunder dilutes your attention, marketing dollars, positioning, messaging, and product sharpness, and is easy to avoid.
